content:
Earlier this year, I replaced the petrol lawn mower at home with a robotic mower that can be controlled via iPhone. All you need to do is manually drive the robot around your garden once with your iPhone, and the system will build a virtual map. Once set up, it will mow automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried out another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe this system may be more convenient and easier to use for many people.

Automatic camera mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I previously reviewed is how each understands your garden.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my phone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. It has three built-in cameras that can automatically map out the lawn area, with no need to bury boundary wires underground, and no extra RTK antenna required.

The automatic initial mapping process clearly takes longer. But I think this method may be simpler for people who are not very tech-savvy.

To test this idea, my mother, who lives in another state, set up and used the TerraMow V1000 entirely on her own, without asking me for any help at all. She replied that everything was working normally. Honestly, I was quite doubtful at the time whether she would have the patience to manually drive the robot along the boundary and then manually mark no-go zones.

Automatic mapping caused one small issue in my front yard. Since there is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn within my map's coverage area.

I solved this by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there is no clearly visible dividing line between two lawns, extra care is needed during the initial mapping stage.

Seeing the world through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of the features I have always loved most. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to cast the feed to a larger window. I could sit comfortably indoors and watch the mower cross the backyard from its own point of view.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun, and sometimes explains why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 has no similar camera streaming feature.

The two iPhone apps are otherwise fairly similar. Both let you schedule work times, adjust mowing patterns, divide zones, mark no-go areas, and remotely control the mower.

Speaking of remote control, TerraMow's design is particularly impressive. In addition to the traditional left/right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone in a normal posture and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with a phone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run entirely on schedule with no human intervention. But TerraMow's joystick is very handy for touching up missed spots.

Sometimes it almost feels like telepathically controlling the robot (and it's quite satisfying). I can hold my iPhone by my side and, with just slight thumb movements, send the machine to wherever I want it to go.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control method.

More aggressive mowing performance

To me, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was noticeably louder while running.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow noisy, but the difference between the two is very obvious. The Anthbot can run extremely quietly — even mowing at night with its headlights on, it's easy to forget it's still operating.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably, so scheduling daytime mowing becomes even more important.

Out of the box, the V1000 feels solid and substantial, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a garage with the product to cover the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow operates reliably and performs consistently. I relied on it for several weeks in a row and never had to do any routine mowing myself.

When smart mapping becomes too smart

The same kind of visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up sometimes backfires.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each mowing run takes a certain amount of time, during which you can't perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain in a row, I ran into an interesting special situation. Some parts of the garden had standing water, and TerraMow cleverly avoided that area during its next run.

Inside the skipped circular area, weeds grew taller and taller. As time went on, the mower seemed to treat these taller patches as targets to keep avoiding, and even after the water had long receded, that patch of grass was never mowed again.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the mower through the overgrown patch, and the problem was resolved immediately. Once that area looked like a normal lawn again, automatic mowing resumed as usual.

Regularly trimming the edges also helps TerraMow handle boundaries more decisively. If tall grass grows in places where the dividing line is blurred, it may be mistaken for an obstacle and excluded from the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less flexible and more reliant on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work, but at the same time avoids the situation where the map "changes its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac review

After trying out both systems, I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera approach to most people.

For me, underground boundary wires were never on the table from the start, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining extra hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, hard-to-recognise boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once wrongly treated tall grass as a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues are solvable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable and consistent automatic mowing, fun live camera footage, and the best manual control experience I've seen in any robotic mower app.

I actually quite enjoy gardening, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that job over to a robot lets me spend more time on landscaping, trimming, and detail work, while keeping the lawn neat and tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 performs excellently in this regard, enough for me to recommend it, especially for people who want a robotic mower but don't want to dig trenches to lay wires, set up an RTK antenna, or walk the entire garden boundary holding a phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon and the official website, priced at $999, with a $200 discount offer. You can also purchase it through the TerraMow official website.
